summary: Pre-Congestion Notification (PCN) protects quality of service for inelastic flows in a Diffserv domain by marking packets when traffic rates pass configured levels. This informational RFC gives an overview of the ways PCN information was considered for encoding in the IP header.

eli5.summary: Traffic lights mark when a road is getting busy before a jam. This memo looks at the different ways to write that sign inside a packet.

questions: how is pcn information encoded in ip headers
how does pcn protect network quality
subtitle: How to mark packets when networks get busy but before they break.

tldr.problem: Networks need to warn of congestion before packets get lost, to help admission control and flow termination decisions. Marking packets requires encoding this information in IP headers alongside other existing uses.
tldr.mechanism: Pre-Congestion Notification (PCN) marks packets using the DSCP and ECN fields when traffic rates exceed configured thresholds. Different encoding schemes use these fields to represent multiple marking states.
tldr.outcome: The working group standardized the 3-in-1 encoding (RFC 6660) which uses a single DSCP to represent three PCN marking states, consolidating previous experimental approaches.

today: RFC 6627 is Informational and summarizes the working group's exploration of PCN encodings. The group standardized the 3-in-1 encoding in RFC 6660, which obsoletes the earlier baseline encoding in RFC 5696.

sections.title: Introduction to PCN Marking
sections.content: Pre-Congestion Notification (PCN) protects quality of service (QoS) for inelastic flows—like video or voice calls that cannot slow down gracefully—by marking packets before a link becomes congested. On every link in a PCN-domain, routers meter traffic and mark PCN-packets when traffic rates exceed configured threshold rates and excess rates. Egress nodes read these marks to make two decisions: whether to admit new flows (admission control) and whether to drop existing flows during serious congestion (flow termination). This gives the network early warning of potential overload, before any packets are actually lost.
sections.eli5: Traffic lights warn drivers that a road is getting busy. PCN marks packets to warn routers about network congestion before it happens.

sections.title: Three Marking Approaches
sections.content: The PCN working group explored three main ways to implement marking. Dual Marking (DM) activates both threshold-marking and excess-traffic-marking on all links, marking traffic into three states: not-marked (NM), threshold-marked (ThM), and excess-traffic-marked (ETM). Egress nodes measure the rates of each state and use them for robust admission control. Single Marking (SM) uses only excess-traffic-marking, requiring only two codepoints (NM and ETM), and is simpler to deploy but less accurate. Packet-Specific Dual Marking (PSDM) distinguishes whether traffic is subject to threshold-marking or excess-traffic-marking, enabling lightweight probing through signaling messages rather than dedicated probe packets.
sections.eli5: Different ways to label cars: DM labels them as not-crowded, somewhat-crowded, or very-crowded. SM just labels not-crowded or very-crowded. PSDM labels them based on what kind of traffic they are.

sections.title: Encoding Constraints and Challenges
sections.content: PCN must encode marking information in two places in the IP header: the Differentiated Services (DS) field—a 6-bit DSCP—and the Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) field—a 2-bit field. The DS field identifies that traffic is subject to PCN-metering; the ECN field carries the actual PCN mark. The main constraint is scarcity: there are only a handful of unused DSCPs in the Internet, so PCN encoding should use at most one additional DSCP per original DSCP. Another challenge is tunneling: when packets are encapsulated, the ECN field must survive the journey through the tunnel and emerge with the mark intact, depending on the tunneling mode (limited-functionality, full-functionality, IPsec, or the newer RFC 6040 rules). Egress nodes must also restore the original ECN field or DSCP, which can be done by signaling, tunneling, or using multiple DSCPs per traffic class.
sections.eli5: The warning marks are tiny (only 8 bits to work with), shared with other purposes in the header, and must survive being wrapped in tunnel headers. It is like writing a tiny note on a postcard that must not get lost even if the postcard is put in an envelope.

sections.title: Encoding Options and Trade-offs
sections.content: Four main encodings emerged. Baseline encoding (RFC 5696) redefines the ECN field with a Not-PCN codepoint, an NM codepoint, an experimental (EXP) codepoint, and a PCN-marked (PM) codepoint. It works well with IPsec tunnels but supports only SM-PCN. 3-in-1 encoding (RFC 6660) extends baseline to encode three states in one DSCP using all four ECN codepoints: NM, threshold-marked, excess-traffic-marked, and a spare. It supports the preferred DM approach and also SM, but requires RFC 6040 tunneling rules to work correctly across tunnels. 3-in-2 encoding uses two DSCPs to carry the three marks and works with legacy tunnel implementations, but consumes more DSCP space. PSDM encoding uses four ECN codepoints across one DSCP and works well with IPsec tunnels, but requires signaling protocol support.
sections.eli5: Baseline is like using one bit to say busy-or-not. 3-in-1 uses both bits to say not-busy, a-little-busy, or very-busy. 3-in-2 uses two address labels to hold all three states. PSDM uses both bits but in a special way.

sections.title: Standardization Outcome
sections.content: The PCN working group initially planned to build experimental encodings on a baseline, but after RFC 6040 standardized ECN tunneling rules, the group decided on a cleaner approach: obsolete the baseline encoding and standardize only the 3-in-1 encoding as a new Standards Track RFC. This consolidated the technical exploration documented in this memo into a single, recommended solution for networks deploying PCN.
sections.eli5: The group tried many ideas, then picked the best one—3-in-1—and made it the official standard.
